regions.name: Brittany
regions.lead: A coast of salt, seaweed and buckwheat, where butter is salted on purpose.
tastes: Mussels grown on poles (moules de bouchot)
regions.habit: The crêperie as village table: a hot griddle, simple flour, and whatever the farm and the sea have to offer that day.

regions.name: Normandy
regions.lead: Orchards, pasture and cream: the great kitchen of apples and cows.
tastes: Cider and perry from old orchard varieties
Camembert de Normandie made with raw milk
regions.habit: The trou normand: a pause in the middle of a long meal for a small glass of calvados.

regions.name: Alsace
regions.lead: A border cuisine, Germanic in spirit and French in finesse, built around the cellar and the preserving jar.
tastes: Riesling and Pinot Gris at the table
regions.habit: The winstub: a tavern with shared tables, a short menu and a local wine poured by the carafe.

regions.name: Burgundy
regions.lead: Where the idea of terroir was refined, one vineyard plot at a time.
regions.habit: The long lunch where the wine is chosen for the dish, and the dish for the wine.

regions.name: Lyon and the Rhône
regions.lead: A city of silk weavers and women cooks, and the capital of generous, unpretentious food.
regions.habit: The bouchon and the mâchon: a hearty, convivial mid-morning meal, historically for working people.

regions.name: Provence
regions.lead: Sun, olive trees and wild herbs, with a cuisine that runs on oil, vegetables and patience.
regions.habit: The morning market, where the menu is decided by what looks best on the stall.

regions.name: The Southwest
regions.lead: The land of duck, beans and brandy, built on the art of preserving through the winter.
regions.habit: The winter store: pots of confit kept in their own fat, ready for the coldest weeks.

regions.name: Auvergne
regions.lead: A volcanic highland of cheese, lentils and potatoes that fed mountain people through hard winters.
tastes: Aligot, the stretchy potato and cheese dish
regions.habit: The buron: the stone hut where summer cheese was made on the high pastures.

recipes.title: Potato gratin
recipes.sub: Gratin dauphinois, with no cheese and no butter.

ingredients.t: A few gratings of fresh nutmeg

steps: Slice the potatoes 2 to 3 mm thick. Do not rinse them: the starch is what thickens the cream.
Rub a baking dish with a cut garlic clove. Crush the remaining garlic into the milk and cream, then add the salt and nutmeg and warm gently.
Layer the potatoes in the dish and pour over the warm milk and cream until they are just covered.
Bake at 160°C (140°C fan) for about 1 hour 15 minutes, until a knife slides in easily and the top is amber.
recipes.changed: The classic already has no cheese. The modern touch is milk alongside the cream, which keeps it silky without the heaviness, and the cut garlic that perfumes the dish without sitting in it.

recipes.title: Lyonnaise salad
recipes.sub: The bouchon favourite, with the bacon fat doing the work of the oil.
steps: Cut the bread into cubes. Cook the lardons in a dry pan over medium heat until golden, then lift them out.
Fry the bread cubes in the rendered fat until crisp, then lift them out too.
Poach the eggs in barely simmering water for 3 minutes.
Take the pan off the heat. Pour in the vinegar and scrape up the browned bits, then stir in the finely sliced shallot. This is your warm dressing.
Toss the frisée with the warm dressing, lardons and croutons. Top with the eggs.
recipes.changed: The classic often adds oil, mustard and herbs. Here the lardon fat is the oil and the vinegar is the seasoning, so there is nothing to hide behind.

recipes.title: Onion soup
recipes.sub: Gratinée, without stock cubes or flour.
steps: Slice the onions thinly. Melt the butter in a heavy pot, add the onions and the salt, and cook on low heat for about 45 minutes, stirring now and then, until deep amber.
Pour in the wine, scrape the bottom of the pot, and let it reduce by half.
Add about 250 ml of hot water per person and simmer for 20 minutes.
Ladle into ovenproof bowls, top with toasted bread and the grated Comté, and grill until bubbling and brown.
recipes.changed: No beef stock, no flour. The patient caramelisation of the onions gives the soup its body, and Comté replaces the usual Gruyère for a nuttier, more local note.

recipes.title: Mussels with Muscadet
recipes.sub: Moules marinières, trimmed to what the sea already provides.

ingredients.n: Muscadet or other dry white wine

steps: Rinse the mussels and discard any that stay open when tapped.
Soften the finely chopped shallots in the butter for 2 minutes. Add the wine and boil for 1 minute.
Tip in the mussels, cover, and steam over high heat for 4 to 5 minutes, shaking the pot, until they open.
Add the pepper and chopped parsley and serve in the pot with all the juices and good bread.
recipes.changed: No cream and no garlic. The briny mussel liquor, the wine and the butter make a sauce that needs no salt and no help.

recipes.title: Normandy chicken with cider
recipes.sub: Poulet vallée d'Auge, without the flambé and the long shopping list.
steps: Pat the thighs dry and season with the salt. Brown them skin-side down in the butter for about 8 minutes until deep gold, then set aside.
In the same pan, brown the apple wedges for 3 minutes.
Pour in the cider and scrape the pan. Return the chicken, cover, and simmer very gently for 30 minutes.
Lift out the chicken, stir the crème fraîche into the sauce and reduce for a few minutes, then pour back over the chicken.
recipes.changed: The classic Vallée d'Auge version adds calvados, shallots and sometimes mushrooms. Here the cider alone carries the flavour, with the apples giving natural sweetness.

recipes.title: Thin apple tart
recipes.sub: Tarte fine aux pommes, five ingredients and one sheet of pastry.
steps: Heat the oven to 200°C. Lay the pastry on a tray and prick it with a fork, leaving a 2 cm border.
Slice the apples thinly and fan them in overlapping rows. Dot with the butter and sprinkle with the sugar.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, until the pastry is deep golden and the edges of the apples have caramelised.
Squeeze the lemon over the hot tart and serve warm.
recipes.changed: No custard base and no apricot glaze. A squeeze of lemon at the end gives the brightness the glaze used to provide.
